title: Turn 7: cast The Ur-Dragon, or cast the Dragon that builds the board?

board.you: Turn 7, precombat main, life 34. Battlefield: Urza's Incubator (Dragon named), Dragon's Hoard with two gold counters, Dragon Tempest, and eight lands covering all five colours. Nine mana available. Hand: The Ur-Dragon, Miirym Sentinel Wyrm, Heroic Intervention. No creatures — your two early Dragons traded away. The Ur-Dragon costs {2}{W}{U}{B}{R}{G} with Incubator, since eminence discounts other Dragon spells and not itself. Miirym costs {G}{U}{R}: Incubator takes {2} and eminence takes {1}.
board.table: Player 2, Azorius control, has five untapped lands and has countered two spells this game. Player 3, Selesnya tokens, is wide but not lethal. Player 4, Rakdos aggro, is at 24 and has been attacking Player 2 every turn.

scenario.question: The commander is castable this turn with two mana left for Heroic Intervention — but the control seat has five untapped and a counter habit. Do you jam the commander with the trick held, cast Miirym for three and keep the commander in the zone, or play nothing and pass with nine open?

branches.choice: Jam The Ur-Dragon now, holding Heroic Intervention
branches.line: Cast The Ur-Dragon for {2}{W}{U}{B}{R}{G} off eight lands plus Dragon's Hoard, keeping {1}{G} for Heroic Intervention through your next attack step. Attack with nothing this turn; the body is summoning-sick.
branches.signals: A nine-mana turn from the five-colour seat is the loudest announcement available to you. Player 2's five untapped lands are the whole question, and Rakdos pressure is the only thing making them spend rather than hold.
branches.coalition_risk: High. A resolved commander with no board behind it makes you archenemy for a body that has not attacked yet — and if the next rotation brings a sweeper you have spent your one big turn on a creature that did nothing.
branches.coaching: Heroic Intervention does not protect the cast. It gives hexproof and indestructible to permanents you control, and a commander on the stack is a spell, not a permanent — a counter beats the whole line and your two held mana were a bluff. The deck's answers on the stack are Deflecting Swat and Flawless Maneuver, and neither is in this hand, so the jam is naked. Countered, the commander hits the graveyard, a state-based action returns it to the command zone, and the next cast carries {2} more — nine mana again even with Incubator. Now the larger point: the pod run measured this commander dealing damage at all in 25 of 100 games and reaching 21 on one defender in 2, and the goldfish casts it by turn six in 4.1% at a mean of 8.172. It is a body, not a payoff. Staking your one realistic window on Player 2's worst-case holding buys a card the deck does not win with.

citations.quote: “Hexproof” on a permanent means “This permanent can’t be the target of spells or abilities your opponents control.”
If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone.
A commander cast from the command zone costs an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game.

branches.choice: Cast Miirym for three; keep the commander in the command zone
branches.line: Cast Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm for {G}{U}{R} — Incubator takes {2} off, eminence takes {1} — keeping six mana up with Heroic Intervention live. The commander stays where eminence works from. Next turn it is still {2}{W}{U}{B}{R}{G}, cast into whatever interaction is left.
branches.signals: Three mana with six open reads as efficient rather than lethal, and ward {2} taxes any targeted answer. If Player 2 counters it, that is their third counter of the game and you cast the commander next turn into a lighter hand.
branches.coalition_risk: Medium. Miirym announces the doubling engine and tables that have seen stack 002 respect it — but a lone Miirym is not archenemy while the token board is the visible threat and Rakdos keeps hitting Player 2.
branches.coaching: This is the sequencing rule played straight: the scariest piece goes last. Both outcomes improve your turn, which is what a probe is for. A counter spent here clears the path. A resolved Miirym is worth more than the commander is: Dragon Tempest is already down, so the next nontoken Dragon you cast is copied and both entries are priced in damage — that board is one permanent short of the four that stack 002 resolves at 64 damage in twelve separately aimed instances, enough to kill a seat at 40. Keep Heroic Intervention for a turn when you control permanents worth protecting, which is the only kind of turn it works on. And you give up nothing by waiting: eminence has been discounting your Dragons from the command zone since turn one and keeps doing it whether the nine-mana body ever lands or not.

citations.quote: “Hexproof” on a permanent means “This permanent can’t be the target of spells or abilities your opponents control.”

branches.choice: Play nothing; pass with nine mana up
branches.line: Pass the turn with nine mana available, representing interaction you do not have — Heroic Intervention is the only instant in hand. Wait for Player 2 to tap out against Selesnya or Rakdos before committing anything.
branches.signals: A five-colour deck passing with nine open reads as a held haymaker, and nobody at this table believes you are a draw-go deck. Player 2 keeps holding counters at no cost, which is exactly what they want to be doing.
branches.coalition_risk: Low this turn, rising every turn after. Each passive rotation is a free draw step for three opponents, and the Selesnya board goes from wide-not-lethal to lethal while you add nothing.
branches.coaching: Audit what you are protecting. Dragon Tempest pays only for arrivals after it, so a turn with no arrival is a turn it is a blank enchantment; nothing in this hand is a kill, and both proven boards need one more permanent than you have. Waiting is defensible only if you concretely expect the Rakdos pressure to force a tap-out inside a turn or two — that is a read about Player 2, not a fact, and Branch B buys the same effect with a threat attached, because ward {2} forces a decision instead of letting the control player make none. The pod run is blunt about the cost: what separated your twelve wins from your 88 losses was land drops and the casts they buy — 7.25 against 5.24, difference 2.01, ci95 [0.52, 3.50], permutation p 0.0002, n=100, every seat a Forge AI. A turn you spend holding is a turn you are not converting mana into board.

recommendation.choice: Cast Miirym for three; keep the commander in the command zone
recommendation.rationale: The commander is an event, not a plan: goldfish mean cast turn 8.172, by turn six 4.1%, never inside ten turns in 7,170 of 10,000 — and in 100 seeded Forge games it dealt commander damage at all in 25 and reached 21 on one defender in 2. So the one cast you get should not be spent as a probe. Miirym at three mana is the cheapest probe available and wins either way: a counter spent clears the path, and a resolved Miirym plus the Dragon Tempest already down is one permanent short of stack 002's board, which deals 64 damage in twelve separately aimed instances and kills a seat at 40. Jamming stakes the turn on Heroic Intervention doing something it cannot — hexproof protects permanents, and a commander on the stack is a spell. Passing donates a rotation to three opponents while you hold no engine piece. Sequence the scariest piece last.
